rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.
Change only gradient duration to test whether the tightly clustered early peaks separate with a shallower slope. This also measures the resolution–time tradeoff before trimming the solvent window.
Keep the shallower gradient and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the early cluster. Higher temperature should also reduce the last-peak time and its score penalty.

At 60 C only one pair remains unresolved, with nearly a minute of headroom before the time penalty begins. Lengthen the gradient one step to measure that pair’s slope response while aiming to keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so shift the starting organic fraction upward while keeping a similar slope to injection 3. This tests solvent-window selectivity and should shorten the run; the first peak will be monitored for excessive loss of retention.
Injection 5 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark and test a shorter gradient. Reducing tG by one step may preserve full resolution while bringing the last peak out earlier.
Shorten the gradient another step to locate the full-resolution speed limit. Injection 6 remains a maximum-score fallback if either early critical pair drops below R = 1.5.

Back off the excessive steepness of injection 7 by lowering phi1 while keeping the eight-minute gradient. This intermediate slope should restore the two marginal resolutions and elute the last peak sooner than injection 6.

Test a one-step temperature decrease at the fastest fully resolved method to measure selectivity sensitivity in the early cluster. This will show whether temperature adjustment can create resolution headroom for further gradient shortening.

Return to 60 C and shift the solvent window upward while preserving injection 8’s slope. This tests whether a higher starting organic fraction can shorten retention and improve the limiting pair without excessively compressing the other early peaks.

The higher starting fraction compressed one early pair below baseline resolution. Test a lower starting fraction with a slightly steeper slope to see whether the early cluster can remain resolved at a shorter last-peak time than injection 8.

Test a slope between the fully resolved injection 8 and marginal injection 7 using a shorter, narrower gradient. The final organic fraction remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, while this grid setting probes the fastest full-resolution boundary.

Injection 12 is marginally unresolved despite its rounded CRF, so injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method. Test the opposite temperature extreme to look for a different elution order that could support a faster, fully resolved gradient.

Return to 60 C and use a shallower gradient to recover the early-pair resolution lost at phi0 = 0.20. This tests whether the higher starting fraction can support full resolution with a useful margin while keeping all peaks within 10 minutes.

The higher starting fraction offers no speed advantage once its critical pair is resolved, so return to phi0 = 0.15. Test a shallower, trimmed gradient to increase the resolution margin while retaining the maximum CRF and keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Shorten injection 15 by one duration step to recover speed while retaining a slightly shallower slope than injection 8. This should provide a fully resolved alternative near six minutes with more margin than the marginally unresolved injection 12.
Reduce the slope one grid step from injection 14 to bring its R = 1.47 pair above 1.5. This tests a second fully resolved solvent window, with the last peak expected comfortably before 10 minutes.

With the maximum score already secured, test whether a shallower gradient at phi0 = 0.20 gives a larger minimum-resolution margin while keeping the last peak under 10 minutes. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Refine around the fastest fully resolved method, injection 8, by lowering the endpoint one step. The slightly shallower slope should add resolution margin with only a modest retention-time increase, preserving the maximum CRF.

Test the remaining endpoint step between fully resolved injection 8 and under-resolved injection 7 to pinpoint the speed boundary. This may shorten the last-peak time below six minutes, though the limiting pair is expected to be close to R = 1.5.

Injection 20 confirms that further steepening loses full resolution, so retain injection 8 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method. Test a slightly shallower gradient for a larger resolution margin while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test whether the higher-starting-organic method from injection 17 remains fully resolved at a temperature one step lower. Its critical-pair pattern differs from injection 8, so this checks an alternative selectivity window while the maximum-score methods remain secured.

Lower the endpoint one step from injection 22 to recover its two marginal early-pair resolutions. This should test a fully resolved 55 C alternative while keeping the last peak below the time-penalty threshold; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 23 to try to lift its remaining critical pair above R = 1.5, while raising the endpoint to ensure late-peak elution. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially securing a maximum-score alternative at 55 C.

Use the final injection to test a trimmed-window method between injections 15 and 21, targeting full resolution with more margin than the fastest method and a last peak near seven minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved option.
